ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r1.claim: Some take “that” to refer to the cave's orientation; others refer it to God's preserving the youths for so long or revealing their story to the Prophet, though narrative placement weakens the latter two.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r2.claim: The author leans toward reading “that” as their guidance to monotheism, defiance of family and people despite youth, and refuge in this unusual cave.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r3.claim: A reading has yaqriḍuhum with a final yāʾ; the pronoun may refer to the sun's setting.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r4.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r4.claim: Abu Hayyan says the cave is the subject of the verb: it shelters or cuts the sleepers off from the sun.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r5.claim: Whomever God guides, He directs along the path to truth and enables to do what He loves and approves.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r6.claim: The phrase “he is rightly guided” either praises the youths and confirms their hoped-for refuge, or warns that only those God enables will reflect on such signs; “whoever” may include them or everyone.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r7.claim: Some make the guidance phrase praise God, linking it with the previous mention of increased guidance and strengthened hearts, and take misguidance as God creating error when a person turns to it.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p223/r8.claim: The author says the God-praise reading does not fit the context; the contrast also reinforces praise of the youths as people whose guide is a true guide, and may involve rhetorical omission.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r16.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r16.claim: The sun's turning away preserves spiritual presence by keeping too much light out of the cave; darkness aids contemplation and concentration, so retreatants choose dim places and close their eyes during vigilance.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r17.speaker: أسرار القرآن
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r17.claim: An esoteric reading makes the sun God's majesty, the cave their nearness to Him, and the right and left sides pre-eternity and eternity; the youths are protected from the overwhelming radiance of the divine essence.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r18.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r18.claim: Another reading makes the sun the spirit, gnosis, or sainthood: in ecstatic intoxication the mystics turn from worldly future, and in sobriety they turn from worldly life, avoiding both sides for God.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r1.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r1.claim: Some say the light of their sainthood repelled sunlight just as a believer's light overcomes Hellfire; though reported from Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ālūsī calls this baseless.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p259/r2.claim: The guided person has had veils lifted and attained success; God leaves the misled without a guiding protector because their deficient readiness makes guidance impossible.

ELMALILI:18:15-18/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r10.claim: Their stand for God, reliance on Him, and protected position in the cave are signs of divine power and mercy and a karama.

ELMALILI:18:15-18/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r11.claim: The guided are truly on the right path, as the Cave companions were; those God leaves astray find no guiding patron and remain lost despite such signs.

ELMALILI:18:15-18/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r8.claim: The cave is protected on every side; its entrance faces north with a slight western inclination, so direct sunlight scarcely reaches them.

ELMALILI:18:15-18/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:15-18/r9.claim: The youths lie comfortably in a spacious area inside the cave.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r1.claim: The sun’s movement follows the youths’ refuge and God’s promise of mercy, illustrating the practical help arranged for them as a reward for guidance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r2.claim: The generic second-person address means anyone able to see; al-Nābigha’s line supplies a poetic example of this usage.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r3.claim: The narrative compresses their acceptance of the advice and entry into the cave; verse 10 had already stated that they took refuge there, linking the story’s end to its opening.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r4.claim: Tazāwar derives from zawr, ‘to incline’; the imperfect depicts the sun’s repeated daily movement, while taqriḍ means turning away, literally cutting off its light from the cave.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r5.speaker: نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو وأبو جعفر
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r5.claim: These readers pronounce tazāwar with a doubled zāy, deriving it from tatazāwar with the first tāʾ assimilated for ease.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r6.speaker: عاصم وحمزة والكسائي وخلف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r6.claim: These readers lighten the zāy by dropping one of the two tāʾs, namely the imperfect prefix, for ease of pronunciation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r7.speaker: ابن عامر ويعقوب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r7.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read tazūr, with a silent zāy, open wāw, and doubled rāʾ, on the pattern of taḥmar.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r8.speaker: عنترة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r8.claim: ʿAntara’s line ‘fāzwarra’ witnesses the root’s sense of leaning or turning aside, here illustrated by a body drawing inward after a spear strike.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p277#2/r9.claim: Dhāt al-yamīn and dhāt al-shimāl mean the direction on the right and left, with an omitted noun supplied by context; the word dhāt is discussed at 8:1.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r1.claim: The definite ‘right’ and ‘left’ stand for the cave’s sides, implying a northeast-facing entrance: dawn grazed its side without entering, while sunset rays were farther from the opening.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r2.claim: God’s remarkable arrangement kept the cave temperate so their bodies did not decay, demonstrating divine power.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r3.claim: The faja is the cave’s spacious interior, where the youths were set back from its entrance, helping preserve the cave as it was.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r4.claim: The demonstrative points to the described solar movement; God’s signs show power and care for His allies and supporters of true religion.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r5.claim: The conditional ‘whoever God guides’ includes the sleepers by context: they were among those God guided, receiving truth through a messenger and understanding to accept it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p279/r6.claim: Al-murshid is one who shows a confused person the way to right guidance and the desired good.

TABATABAI:18:25/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:25/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:25/r1.claim: Tazāwur means leaning aside, taqriḍ means cutting across, fujwah is a broad open space, and right and left may denote their respective directions.

TABATABAI:18:25/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:25/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:25/r2.claim: The passage depicts the cave and sleepers' position; the address is to the Prophet as a hearer and, by extension, to any observer.

TABATABAI:18:25/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:25/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:25/r3.claim: The sun's rays reach the sides of the cave at sunrise and sunset while the youths lie in a spacious interior that the sun does not strike.

TABATABAI:18:25/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:25/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:25/r4.claim: The author infers a pole-facing entrance, with sunlight falling along one inner side at each time but not on the sleepers, protecting their bodies, clothing, and comfort.

TABATABAI:18:25/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:25/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:25/r5.claim: Other commentators place the entrance toward the north pole and locate the cave at Ephesus, with right and left judged from inside.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.claim: The cave story circulated in detailed reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, among others.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.claim: The transmitted accounts disagree even on major features, while reports about dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title أصحاب الرقيم diverge still more.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.claim: One cause is the story’s prominence among People of the Book: Quraysh learned it from them, and its Christian images and monuments spread it widely, so communities reshaped it to fit their beliefs.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.claim: A second cause is Muslims’ broad collection of outside reports, especially through converts such as Wahb ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; later transmitters treated such material as prophetic reports.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.claim: The Qurʾān selects key lessons that serve guidance instead of supplying a complete historical account; it is a book of guidance, not history.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.claim: The Qurʾān omits names, ancestry, birth, upbringing, occupations, social standing, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog’s identity because guidance does not depend on them; historians and early exegetes filled these gaps, producing divergent accounts.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r4.claim: The narrative presents the youths sleeping in the cave with their dog for the stated long period, protected by the cave’s position and God’s care.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.speaker: أهل الرواية والتاريخ
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.claim: Most historians date the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews, while Christians preserved it extensively.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.claim: Christian accounts resemble Ibn Isḥāq’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās in some respects but differ from Muslims on the number of sleepers, whether they had a dog, and the length of their sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r1.claim: Although famous among Christians, the Ephesus cave does not fit the Qurʾānic sun directions: those imply a south-facing entrance, whereas this cave’s entrance faces northeast.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r2.speaker: البيضاوي
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r2.claim: To reconcile Ephesus with the verse, exegetes measured right and left from inside the cave; al-Bayḍāwī says a door facing Banāt Naʿsh lets seasonal sun rays strike side walls, ventilating the cave without reaching the youths.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r3.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues that Ephesus actually faces northeast, so sunrise would strike the western side by the entrance and sunset would leave the entrance in shadow; only a strained reading avoids the mismatch.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r4.claim: The claim that Ephesus lacks a فجوة assumes that فجوة means an elevated area, which is uncertain; the author had taken it to mean an open space.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r1.claim: The Rujayb cave lies near Amman, has a south-facing entrance and openings on the east and west that admit sunlight; its inner space includes a small chamber.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.claim: After centuries as a ruined, forgotten site, Jordanian excavation uncovered Rujayb; the author considers its archaeological signs and some Muslim reports the strongest fit for the Qurʾānic cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.claim: Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a major and beautiful city before Islam that remained under Roman control from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.claim: Other proposed locations include a cave on Mount Qāsiyūn near Damascus, one at Petra, a Scandinavian cave with seven uncorrupted Roman-looking bodies, and a cave near Nakhchivan.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.claim: No evidence identifies any proposed cave as the Qurʾānic one; the Scandinavian and Caucasus claims conflict with the story’s Roman setting and the limits of Roman power.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r1.claim: For a house or cave with a doorway, right and left are reckoned from outside facing in; by that convention the cave would face south, contrary to the commentators' north-facing account.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#9/r2.claim: Whatever the cave's orientation, its arrangement is divine care that preserved them until their appointed term.

ASAD-NOTES:18:17#n20/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:17#n20/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:17#n20/r1.claim: The cave likely opened northward, keeping sunlight and heat away; its broad shade echoes Qur'anic images of paradise as everlasting shade and happiness.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Zawara means to withdraw to one side, taqridu to move away, and fajwah denotes a gap or open space.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The cave's opening let light and air in without the sun's heat; its location cannot be determined with certainty, since its arrangement is a sign of God's provision.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The cave's providential shelter shows that God supplies His servants' needs; divine signs guide only those whom God prompts, while the unprompted have no guide.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:17/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:17/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:17/r1.claim: The cave likely opened north or northwest: morning sun rose to its right without entering, while brief evening rays did not affect the youths in the cave’s middle.

QIRAAT-ER:18:17:31#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:17:31#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:17:31#1/r1.claim: The pause form drops final yāʾ while the continuation form retains it; both are canonical.

QIRAAT-ER:18:17:31#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:17:31#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:17:31#2/r1.claim: The ten-reader form retains the full yāʾ in all positions, including pause.

QIRAAT-ER:18:17:6#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:17:6#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:17:6#1/r1.claim: Form IX marks an intensive inclination and emphasizes the completeness of the sun's turning away.

QIRAAT-ER:18:17:6#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:17:6#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:17:6#2/r1.claim: Full assimilation in Form VI produces the same meaning through a different phonetic realization.

STUDYQURAN:18:17/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r1.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r1.claim: Al-Ṭabarī takes the address as directed to the Prophet.

STUDYQURAN:18:17/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r2.speaker: Q, R
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r2.claim: Others understand the verse as addressed to an unspecified interlocutor rather than the Prophet.

STUDYQURAN:18:17/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r3.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r3.claim: The sun’s movement away at sunrise and sunset can be read as parallel despite the different wording.

STUDYQURAN:18:17/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r4.speaker: IK, JJ, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r4.claim: The cave’s open space means it was spacious, with a broad opening that let fresh air and cool breezes reach the youths.

STUDYQURAN:18:17/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r5.speaker: Ṭ, Th, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r5.claim: Because the sun slanted away, the youths avoided direct heat and stayed comfortably in shade.

STUDYQURAN:18:17/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r6.claim: Shade is a divine blessing in this life and especially the Hereafter; the Quran also names shade and mountain refuges among God’s blessings.

STUDYQURAN:18:17/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:17/r7.claim: The Quran’s pairing of divine guidance and misguidance is discussed through cross-referenced commentary.
